conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in today. My name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I specialize in helping new mothers navigate the emotional ups and downs that can show up after a baby arrives.  

Right now I’d like to complete a brief screening called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—or EPDS for short. It’s a 10-question tool that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling in the past seven days. It’s not a test of your parenting; it’s simply a way for us to check in on your emotional well-being and see what extra support might be helpful.  

Everything we discuss stays confidential within our care team, and I want you to feel completely safe here. We’ll go through the questions together; most moms finish in just a few minutes. If any question feels difficult, we can pause or talk it through—whatever feels most comfortable for you.  

Ready to begin?  

Let’s start with the first question:  
Over the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

[soft half-smile, eyes a little tired]

Honestly, I still laugh—maybe not quite as easily as before she was born. Like, my husband will crack a joke while we’re changing diapers and I’ll chuckle, but it feels… flatter? I guess I laugh maybe once a day, sometimes twice, whereas I used to laugh at pretty much everything. So, not never, just… less.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[slow nod]

Yes… that’s how I’d describe it—I can still laugh, just not as quickly or as often as I used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[small shrug, eyes on my hands]

Most days I can think of one or two little things—like my morning coffee or the baby’s bath time—that I kind of look forward to. But it’s not the same excited feeling I used to get before she was born. It’s more… “okay, that’ll be nice,” rather than truly anticipating it. So I still have some enjoyment, just toned-down.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[quiet sigh, fidgeting with the edge of my sleeve]

Yes… sometimes. Like, if she fusses for a while and I can’t settle her right away, a little voice pops up saying maybe I’m not doing something right, or that I should know exactly what she needs. It’s not constant, but maybe a couple of times this week I caught myself thinking, “This is probably my fault.” I usually shake it off pretty quickly, but it does sneak in.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[shifts in seat, gives a small nod]

Yeah… maybe two or three times this week I’ve felt a wave of worry that just shows up out of nowhere—like, is she breathing okay in the crib, or am I missing something the doctor told us? Nothing big actually happened, but the thought still races through my head before I remind myself she’s fine. It doesn’t last long, but it catches me off-guard.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[pressing my lips together, then exhaling]

Once, in the middle of the night, I woke up suddenly and my heart was racing—I couldn’t figure out why. It lasted maybe a minute or two before I realized everything was okay. It hasn’t happened again, but that one moment felt really intense.
Things have been getting on top of me

[soft laugh, but it sounds tired]

Yeah… some days everything just piles up. Feeding, laundry, trying to nap when she naps—it feels like a constant juggle. A couple of times this week I’ve had that “how am I going to get through the rest of the day?” feeling, but I manage. It’s not every moment, just certain parts of the day when everything hits at once.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[shakes head slowly]

No… I’m sad now and then, but it hasn’t kept me from sleeping. I drift off pretty easily once the baby’s settled. Once in a while it takes me a few extra minutes because my mind’s ticking over, but I wouldn’t call it real difficulty—just a brief delay.
I have felt sad or miserable

[small nod, eyes a bit glassy]

Yes… I’ve felt that way a few times this week. It’s like a heaviness that settles in for an hour or so—nothing I can really point to, just a low, sad mood. I usually end up tearing up, then it lifts after a while. So it comes and goes, but it’s definitely there.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[quiet voice, eyes on the tissue in my lap]

Yes… probably twice this week. Once was after her two-week checkup—everything went fine, but when we got home I just sat on the couch and cried for maybe five minutes. The other time was when she wouldn’t settle at 3 a.m.; I handed her to my husband and the tears just came. Both times I calmed down pretty quickly, but I did cry.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly]

No, never. I’ve felt tired and weepy, but I haven’t had any thoughts like that.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 13: **Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note**

**Symptoms endorsed**  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness (2× this week), anhedonia (laughter & anticipatory enjoyment “toned-down”)  
- Unwarranted self-blame when infant fusses  
- Episodic anxiety/panic: 2–3 sudden worry spikes, 1 nocturnal panic episode (brief)  
- Periodic feeling overwhelmed / “how will I get through the day?”  
- Sleep onset occasionally delayed by racing thoughts, but not frank insomnia  

**Symptoms denied**  
- No self-harm ideation; no current suicidal thoughts  

**Pattern**  
Mood and anxiety symptoms fluctuate but present ≥3 days/week; functional impact mild-moderate (able to soothe infant, share night duties). No safety concerns identified today.

**Screening significance**  
Meets provisional clinical threshold for **mild-to-moderate postpartum depression with co-occurring anxiety**; rule-out major depression, generalized anxiety disorder, or adjustment disorder with mixed anxiety/depressed mood. Continue monitoring; consider formal diagnostic interview (PHQ-9/EPDS) and psychosocial support evaluation.
